WASHINGTON (CNN) -- Sniper Lee Boyd Malvo said in a letter to CNN that he is still "grappling with shame, guilt, remorse and my own healing if that will ever be possible." And a social worker who has worked extensively with him said he draws self-portraits that often show him with a tear running down his cheek. A self-portrait drawn by sniper Lee Boyd Malvo. Many of his drawings show him with a tear running down his cheek. Malvo, 22, spends 23 hours a day inside his cell at Virginia's toughest prison, a maximum-security compound called Red Onion, not far from the Kentucky border. He's serving a life sentence. According to social worker Carmeta Albarus-Lindo, Malvo is a changed person since he and John Allen Muhammad terrorized the Washington area five years ago this month in attacks that left 10 dead over a 23-day period. "The most I can do is to continue to be there, because that is his greatest fear -- that, you know, another parental figure would abandon him because that was what he'd been exposed to all his life," said Albarus-Lindo, who has spent hundreds of hours with Malvo since his arrest and conviction.  Read the letter » . She said one of those "parental" figures was Muhammad, who met Malvo in the Caribbean nearly two years before the deadly shooting spree began in 2002. Muhammad became the teenager's surrogate father, convincing him that violence was the only way to correct perceived injustices to African-Americans, Albarus-Lindo said. He ordered Malvo to go to bed each night and to memorize passages from "The Art of War," an ancient Chinese text on battlefield strategy. According to Albarus-Lindo, Malvo was "brainwashed" into aiding Muhammad in the murders. However, prosecutors have said Malvo, even at 17, knew what he was doing. "I thought he was coldblooded," said Paul Ebert, commonwealth attorney for Prince William County, Virginia, of the first time he met Malvo. "He was a person who had chosen a life of crime." And when a Virginia jury spared Malvo's life, some investigators said they were horrified. "That was the hardest day of my career," said April Carroll of the Bureau of Alcohol, Firearms and Tobacco. "I felt that day we had failed when Malvo was not sentenced to death." Some of the victims' families said they are content that Malvo did not receive the death penalty. Vicki Buchanan Snyder, whose brother James "Sonny" Buchanan was shot in the back while mowing a patch of lawn at a Maryland auto dealership, said she was "satisfied" with the jury's verdict. As for Malvo, Albarus-Lindo said he will "never forgive himself for what has happened." When she first began seeing him, he still called Muhammad "Dad." It took months, she said, before he stopped. In the interim, Albarus-Lindo said, he took college correspondence courses and began to draw. Muhammad is at a Virginia prison called Sussex One. In a DVD made last year inside prison and obtained exclusively by CNN, he said he is "still fighting" on death row. He wants to "correct," he said, some "inaccurate statements" made by the news media about his relationship with Malvo. He wasn't specific about what he meant.  Watch Muhammad on death row » . Muhammad's ex-wife, Mildred, said she believed that she was the real target of the snipers from the beginning. She and her children live in suburban Washington, and she runs a Web site called Afterthetrauma.org, devoted to the victims of domestic abuse. Mildred Muhammad said she feels her ex-husband wanted to kill her as revenge because she was able to gain custody of their three children. As for his relationship with Malvo, she said she too is convinced that John Allen Muhammad brainwashed the younger man. "That boy was a victim before he even knew it," she said. "His life was over when he said, 'Hi.' " E-mail to a friend .

"He gave him what he never had," the social worker explained, describing how Muhammad exploited Malvo's emotional vulnerabilities to gain complete control over him.

According to the social worker's account, Muhammad employed a systematic process of psychological manipulation that mental health experts have compared to cult indoctrination tactics. Experts in coercive control and cult psychology who have studied the case note that such tactics—isolation, indoctrination, and the exploitation of a young person's need for belonging and paternal approval—are hallmarks of psychological manipulation that can override an adolescent's developing sense of right and wrong.

## Prosecutors Maintain Malvo Knew What He Was Doing

The network's extensive reporting captured the unprecedented atmosphere of fear that gripped the nation's capital and surrounding suburbs in Maryland and Virginia. Schools canceled outdoor activities, gas stations installed screens to shield customers, and residents altered their daily routines, walking in zigzag patterns and avoiding open spaces.

The **sniper** attacks, later attributed to John Allen Muhammad and Lee Boyd Malvo, represented one of the most harrowing criminal sprees in modern American history. The perpetrators operated from a modified vehicle, using a hole cut into the trunk to conceal their position while targeting victims from a distance. This method of attack—random, seemingly motiveless, and nearly impossible to predict—created a unique form of psychological terror that extended far beyond the physical danger itself.

Law enforcement agencies from multiple jurisdictions coordinated an intensive manhunt, complicated by the shooters' mobility and the unpredictable nature of their attacks across different locations. The eventual apprehension of the two suspects came after weeks of investigation, tips from the public, and coordinated efforts across state lines.

RED ONION STATE PRISON, Va. — Five years after a string of shootings paralyzed the Washington, D.C. region, Lee Boyd Malvo sits in a maximum-security prison cell, serving multiple life sentences without the possibility of parole.

Malvo, now 22, was 17 years old when he and John Allen Muhammad carried out a series of sniper attacks in October 2002 that left 10 people dead and three others critically wounded across Maryland, Virginia, and Washington, D.C. The shootings brought the region to a standstill, with residents avoiding gas stations, altering routines, and living in fear of an unseen killer.

Muhammad, who was convicted as the mastermind behind the attacks, was executed in 2009. Malvo, spared the death penalty due to his age at the time of the crimes, has spent the years since largely out of the public eye.

According to those who have worked with him, Malvo has reportedly expressed remorse for his role in the killings, describing himself as having been manipulated by Muhammad, whom he has referred to as a father figure.

"He was a child who was groomed and indoctrinated," said a social worker who has met with Malvo during his incarceration and requested anonymity to discuss the case. "That doesn't excuse what happened — nothing does. Ten people are dead. But when you look at what happened to him before the shootings, you start to understand how a teenager ends up doing something like this."

The social worker described Malvo as introspective in the years since the attacks, engaging in therapy and expressing a desire to understand his own psychological state during the shootings.

"He's spoken about feeling like he was in a fog, almost dissociated from his actions at the time," the social worker said. "Now he says he thinks about the victims and their families every day. Whether people believe that or not is up to them."

Prosecutors and victims' families have remained skeptical of any claims of remorse, noting the calculated nature of the attacks, which included the use of a modified vehicle to conceal the shooter and a rifle capable of hitting targets from long distances.

Malvo reportedly spends much of his time reading and has enrolled in prison education programs. He remains housed separately from the general population due to the high-profile nature of his case.

"He understands he's going to die in prison," the social worker said. "There's no getting around what happened. But he's tried, in his own way, to reckon with it."

The families of the victims have largely declined to comment on Malvo's life behind bars, with several stating in past interviews that his fate is of little concern to them compared to the permanent loss they've endured.

As the five-year anniversary of the attacks passes, the D.C. sniper case remains a somber reminder of the three weeks in October 2002 when ordinary activities — pumping gas, mowing lawns, walking to school — became potential moments of danger for millions of people in the region.
